newsitem.title: CUBA: Canadian Foreign Minister to visit Cuba next week.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Foreign Minister to visit Cuba next week.

text.p: Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy will travel to Cuba next Tuesday on what will be the highest-level Canadian visit to the communist-ruled island in two decades, Canadian officials said on Friday.
His planned two-day visit highlights Canada's desire to engage in dialogue with Cuba and its disagreement with the U.S. policy of isolating the communist-ruled nation.

Differences between Washington and Ottawa on Cuba policy have widened since the United States toughened its 35-year-old economic embargo on Cuba last year with the so-called Helms-Burton law, which Canada opposes.
A Canadian Foreign Ministry statement released in Havana said Axworthy would travel with Secretary of State for Latin America and Africa Christine Stewart.
"I welcome this opportunity to review our relations and exchange views on a broad range of issues," Axworthy said in the statement.
"Canada has maintained a long-standing dialogue with Cuba that includes questions of human rights, good governance, trade and economic and legal reform," he said.
While Canada and Cuba did not agree on all issues, "we have chosen to discuss our difference of views in a context of engagement and dialogue," he added.

Axworthy said he would review relations and discuss a wide range of issues, which he did not specify. He was expected to raise Canadian concerns about human rights and democracy with President Fidel Castro's government.
Canada is a leading trade and investment partner of Cuba. Like other U.S. allies, it has objected to parts of the Helms-Burton law that seek to punish foreign firms doing business with the island.
Axworthy's visit follows a trip to Canada last October by deputy Cuban president Carlos Lage.
The last high-level visit by a Canadian to Cuba was by former prime minister Pierre Trudeau in 1976. Axworthy's visit will be the first by a Canadian foreign minister since Castro's 1959 revolution.

Canadian firms are among leading investors in sectors such as mining, oil exploration and tourism, and Canadian tourists are one of the largest group of foreign visitors to the island. Trade in 1995 totalled more than $400 million.
